utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Now Mr. Vasic is going to surprise us with his speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all. I'll do my best; that much is certain. I think a lot depends on the witness and the kind of answers that he provides.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let's start with our questions, please. Bearing in mind the course of our cross-examination yesterday, sir, could I please ask you to try to answer my questions directly. If you don't understand, please state so, but try to give clear answers so that we can get through this as quickly as possible. Thank you. After touring the rooms in which prisoners were being detained, did you order that those rooms be secured, that security be provided for those rooms?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because they were secured already and they remained that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Having toured those rooms, in your security assessment what did you believe to be the most important issues involved in a possible evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried out no security assessment to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: From the moment you gave the order for a number of buses to enter the Velepromet compound and for the prisoners to start boarding -- or rather, do you remember when this was?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This might have been around -- at around 2330 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you order the rooms to be emptied one by one or several rooms all at once?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one by one. I gave the orders to the officers and then the buses, as they were parked in the same order. The bus on which I was was the farthest one from the room that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did each of these buses have two police officers providing security?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two officers escorting the prisoners of war to each of the buses as well as the officers in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you order for the military police to secure the area around the buses?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need because that area was already secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Once the prisoners got on to the buses, where were they taken over by the military police who were providing security along the way?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was in a previous order, an order familiar with Colonel Mrksic, Major Sljivancanin, and the officers in charge of the evacuation and in charge of that column. My duty, as I've pointed out already, was to get the POWs on the buses. And once the buses left the gate, my duty ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You've told us that already. Does that mean that you were not in touch with the unit that took over at the gate?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't know who their commander was or who he was subordinated to, under whose command he was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that during the evacuation Colonel Kijanovic, Major Stosic, and warrant officer -- and a warrant officer were saying that Crevar, Marko and Topola were saying that you were to be killed along with the Ustashas --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was first warranted by warrant officer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time to ensure that all the names get recorded. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They also said --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us about that yesterday. All I wanted to know -- or rather, it was my colleague who asked you and you provided a detailed account of this. Let's not go back to that now. At the time, were you also told that Crevar and Topola had been saying things to the effect that they were all right with the prisoners being taken out of those rooms, except for that one room with the tin door?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Once the evacuation was over, did they not tell you that Crevar and Topola were taking some persons away and that bursts of gun-fire could be heard just outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your testimony before the trial chamber in Belgrade, did you say that you heard they had been taken to the cornfield?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was indeed what I testified, but I did not know there was a cornfield anywhere in the vicinity because I couldn't just go and look.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Having been informed by your subordinates about all these things, you talked to Grabar [phoen] telling him that you were there on behalf of the security administration, the supreme commander, that the prisoners were to go to Sremska Mitrovica? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't a conversation proper, it was a verbal clash, an altercation, if you like. There were raised voices on both sides. Crevar said that he was the one who had taken these people aside, those criminals, as he said, because they -- they were Ustashas who had been killing the Serbian people and that they need to be held accountable, and he was already taking steps against these people he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was your authority or your powers, based on the rules governing your service in this situation where Crevar was making threats against your person and making it impossible for you to carry out your tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to Article 112 on the law on armed forces, under that Article there is an exact description of how the command of the armed forces in the JNA and the TO is to be organised, how the resources are to be used in order to achieve a common or mutual objective. There is the principle of singleness of command, and the next important thing is that the orders given by superior officers must be carried out. An order from a superior officer is law for all of the subordinate officers, which as precisely what I did. What I found there was a duality of command, I mean within the Velepromet compound, and that is why I did what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about your powers under Articles 46 and 45 of the rules governing the work of the security bodies of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all the same as whatever Article 112 envisages, and all the other legal provisions stem from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I respectfully interrupt. If my learned friend is going to ask various questions about, for example, Article 112, as being specified here and also other references to Articles 46 and 45, there are copies available for the witness at this time, if the Court or my learned friend would wish to draw the witness's attention to them or other things as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know we were led into this, Mr. Vasic, by the witness with Article 112, but you have specifically referred him to two articles. And at the moment it would seem appropriate that he have an opportunity to refresh his recollection of them before answering you, if you're going to ask him about the detail of the effect of those two articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but the witness did say yesterday that he was fully aware of the rules of service. I'm about to ask him about his powers and his actions and not about the actual substance of that Article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Article 46 and 45?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not going there. I'm not going to be asking him about the provisions of these rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand your earlier question then, but you ask now what it is you're going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, my question is: Why did you not arrest Marko Crevar when he opposed your order to have the room emptied and when you learned that he had taken prisoners away and killed them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a complex question, if I consider my role in the area. My actions were those that would generally have been taken by any military commander. I acted in keeping with the regulations. I acted in keeping with the rules of military discipline. I acted in keeping with any rules governing the work of military police. I used force in order to accomplish my mission, and I did accomplish my mission. It wasn't my place to arrest the chief of the Vukovar SUP. He did not commit any crimes in my presence. I was warned, however, that certain POWs had been taken away and that bursts of gun-fire had been heard. In addition to this, he clearly stated that he was in charge of these actions. I never knew who had empowered him, who had authorised him to do these things. It may have been Colonel Mrksic for all I know because we were, after all, in Colonel Mrksic's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you said at the outset, you were tasked by the security administration with uncovering war crimes committed by both Croats and the JNA. When you were told that members of the TO and Marko Crevar were taken prisoners outside of the Velepromet compound and that bursts of gun-fire could be heard, would this have provided sufficient grounds for you to arrest Marko Crevar and to verify all this information you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not have constituted sufficient grounds, the reason being that Marko Crevar was in charge of a unit under the command of Vojvoda Topola. Those men were Chetniks. They were getting ready for a possible showdown with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have enough soldiers to stop this unit, to make them follow your orders and --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- and in order to protect the lives of the prisoners and in order to make sure that your mission was completed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many military police officers were there, but I did know that there were officers there going about their tasks in carrying out whatever assignments they had been given by their superiors. Major Sljivancanin, Colonel Mrksic, that for me was sufficient guarantee that I would be able to carry out my own assignment under the protection of those officers and those soldiers that, if I was willing to carry it out and if I had sufficient will-power to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At which point in time did you order the use of force?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ordered the use of force when I first gave one warning and then the other. At this point in time, they threatened to use weapons against me. It was at this point that I called Captain Borisavljevic. His subordinate officers told me that he was not around, which really surprised me. I found it equally surprising that at the most critical moment of all, when Crevar told me he would not allow the Ustashas and criminals to be taken away even if this meant he had to use weapons against us, my fellows from the same operations group, Colonel Tomic and Colonel Stojanovic approached me to say that they did not wish to stay there, that they were about to leave the Velepromet compound altogether, and that they were on their way to see Colonel Mrksic to tell him about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the use of force that you ordered? Did you apply this for the first time when Crevar and Topola made it clear to you that you would not be able to carry out your assignment? Do you think you would have been able to save all of the prisoners if you had decided to act earlier on?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I started to using force when I decided to empty the prisoners from that room and get them on those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you did not use force when you allegedly heard that prisoners were being taken outside the Velepromet compound?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need, and I could not know for sure that this was true and until these facts were verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And when did you verify these facts?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was verified by Colonel Kijanovic in the morning of the 20th of November. I left on a mission with Major Sljivancanin. We were off to the hospital, and Warrant Officer Korica was with us, too. Colonel Kijanovic took a number of military police officers with him, and there was a vehicle that had been assigned to him by Colonel Mrksic. He found out that there was 17 bodies, dead bodies, in the area, which he then collected - he told he about this later on - and took the dead bodies to the military cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether he buried the bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the military cemetery. That's what he said. He certainly would not have been able to do this on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you about the whereabouts of this military cemetery?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say; I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you ordered for that armoured combat vehicle to enter the Velepromet compound, why did you not arrest Crevar and Topola at this point?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had already used sufficient force and sufficient manners by the fact that I started exercising command in the area. If you want me to, I can repeat my account of how exactly this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the fact that you failed to arrest Crevar and Topola did not lead to an increased threat to the life of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think there was any increase in the threat to the lives of the prisoners because they weren't on the buses by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you not say that Topola was drunk, boarded one of the buses and tried to attack you with a knife?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that it was Topola who was drunk. I was calling out names, and I was asking the POWs about their names, trying to record their names in a notebook that I had. It was at this point that Vojvoda Topola got on to the bus in order to settle the accounts with me. He lifted my body. He approached me from behind, he lifted my body into the air, and he put a knife to my throat. If you want me to, I can go over this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've described that for us already. Was even that not sufficient for you to order his arrest, the fact that he attacked you, the fact that after that he tried to attack the prisoners, the fact that there was blood dripping from his knife? All of this was not sufficient for you to order his arrest?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who should I have ordered that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police were there with him securing the room. They were acting in concert. That was before I even got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you saying now that there was nobody to whom you could issue an order at that point to arrest Topola?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been very risky to my own person. I don't believe I would have been a witness here today had I done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As the responsible officer, did you put your life over and above the lives of the men who were threatened?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I first ordered the sergeant --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. You don't want to hear how I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it about the machine-gun being loaded? You told my learned friend about it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I also told him to target me, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us the military policemen, even without your order, evidently took Topola from the bus and held him. Why didn't you arrest him then?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was taken out by Sekic with his two policemen, Second Lieutenant Sekic. I told the Chamber how after the bus left the compound I noticed that Topola had changed into clean overalls. He was no longer blood-stained and in the company of a woman as tall as he was turned up in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you didn't arrest him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You had Topola before you and there were indicia that he might be a war criminal. You had Topola there who had attacked your life and limb while you were carrying out your official duties. Wasn't that sufficient grounds to arrest him or even to kill him when he attacked you with a knife? Weren't you authorised to do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. But he was also authorised to act towards me as he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: May I conclude, then, that you did nothing to prevent or stop the alleged taking out of prisoners after you learned about this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You couldn't conclude that and that would be an insult to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did everything to complete my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that allegedly you heard that people were being taken out. What did you do to stop that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you authorised to protect the prisoners, even if you had to kill the people taking them out?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My authority was first to caution them, according to the military regulations; then to fire in the air, one burst; then the next burst in the legs; and then the following burst in the body. That's according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If your story is true, I conclude then that you're responsible for what happened in Velepromet while you were in command of the evacuation of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed my task and I'm proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You're aware of your omissions, and that's why you're trying to cover them up in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm proud to have completed my task. I completed it on behalf of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll move on. What time was it when you left Velepromet and arrived in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I left Velepromet after 2400 hours. From Velepromet to the command post there are about five kilometres certainly. That's already been said. I know what my soldier's march is like, and I know that I must have marched for about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Negoslavci, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the sign-post saying "Negoslavci" is, but I know where the command post is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you went to the command post?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I looked at the people there. I was very upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw my officers and my men who had abandoned me. I told them they had betrayed me at the most crucial moment, that they had put my life at risk, and I observed what was going on. All I wanted was to see where Colonel Mrksic was so I could approach him and tell him what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You saw your comrades there and you were upset with them. They had placed your life at risk. Did you institute any kind of report against them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Don't insult me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are talking above each other as you go along. The interpreter has no hope of following you. There must be a pause, even if you don't agree with what is being said by the other person, even if you want to put something different, it is necessary that you wait so that the interpreters can complete what is being said. That way, we will manage to record all of what each of you wishes to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness allow me to complete my question; that's why the problem arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to complete my question, then leave a short pause before you start answering, otherwise the interpreters will not be able to follow. I asked you whether you submitted a report to your superior officers about your colleagues who were in your group from the security administration who refused to comply with your order, who abandoned you while you were performing your duty, and who put your life at risk. Did you report them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not submit such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you duty-bound to do so?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you were looking around hoping to spot Colonel Mrksic. Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First he wasn't there. There were other people there. Then he turned up in the ground floor area where we first arrived and where he had met us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the operations room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there is also another small room there which I explained about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you now referring to the operations room or the small room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the big operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In that big operations room, did you address the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who else was in that room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomic, all my comrades, they went in and out. They were milling about, and I was searching for an opportunity to approach Colonel Mrksic and speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was Jerko Crmaric there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, as I said, but at what point in time, I don't know. I first approached Colonel Mrksic, and only then did I meet Colonel Crmaric and talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the duty officer there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Couldn't you have first reported to the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had I done so, I would not have been able to approach Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to leave a short pause between question and answer because the interpreters are having problems. Why do you think you would not have been able to approach Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was always busy. There were many officers there. He had tasks to carry out, so why would I be able to ask for an audience when Slavko Tomic was the officer who was my superior and who was authorised to see him and to receive instructions and orders from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that allegedly you told Mrksic what you had experienced and that people had been killed, and you say that there were quite a few people present in the room but that you don't believe anybody else heard what you were telling him. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anyone heard or not. It wasn't my aim to have other people hear it; I wanted him to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then you must have spoken in a low voice?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke in a normal voice. Sometimes I might raise my voice when speaking to you, and I apologise for that; it's automatic. It simply follows from my feelings when you provoke me like that. I do apologise for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What time was it approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise, but I told you how I got back. There was Jerko Crmaric there, those comrades of mine were there, then we had a meeting with Major Sljivancanin concerning the tasks that had to do with the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Apart from General Crmaric, was Colonel Dusovic [phoen] there; do you know him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him. But I saw that Crmaric was accompanied by two of his colonels who were subordinate to him, probably from some service like logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you say in your statement that as soon as you finished speaking you turned around and left?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have to put it to you that what you said and what you are now saying as regards what you told Colonel Mrksic does not correspond to what you told the Trial Chamber in Belgrade under oath. I will now ask the usher to give you the transcript from the trial before the war crimes court in Belgrade of the 17th of December, 2004, and that's on page 45 in the B/C/S version. And, for my learned friends, on page 28 of the English version. I will read out to you, as it's a dialogue, the relevant part, and you will only tell me whether such a dialogue was conducted before the court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the president of the chamber put your statement to you and say that you then said that the territorials and the volunteers murdered prisoners and that the bodies were next to Velepromet? And your response was: "No, I didn't say that." Then the president of the chamber put it to you: "That statement is in this record." You then replied: "Probably that's what was stated." The president of the Chamber asked you about Djordje Trifunovic, and you replied: "In my statement I said that, but I could say that only after I had learned from Colonel Bozidar Kijanovic that he had undertaken measures and carried out an inspection, that is, on the 20th of November in the morning he inspected the situation around Velepromet and they found about 17 corpses." Is this the dialogue that was conducted before the Trial Chamber in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Mr. Vasic, Your Honours, I -- in connection with the facts being presented here they were checked when I testified before the military court. They were then checked when I testified before the investigators of this Tribunal, and then they were checked when I testified before the special court in Belgrade. Please understand that I am a person who wishes to repeat before this Tribunal what I have already testified to and which I say is the full truth. From the moment I was invited or summoned to the first interview before the military court in Belgrade, I was subjected to pressure. I was summoned to make a statement and to be interviewed as a witness three days after the NATO bombing of buildings in Belgrade and facilities in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I respect the witness's need to explain, but I don't think we have time. He can explain about this statement before the court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can cut it short, but then I have to start with my encounter with Counsel Vasic. One day Counsel Vasic called me through Lieutenant-Colonel Panic who is now a lieutenant-general and asked to meet me in the school centre in order to harmonise some facts in the statements, as they told me. I felt that this was pressure, a continuation of the pressure I had continually been subjected to, and that was the attitude I took towards Counsel Vasic. He was correct but he attempted to exert pressure on me. I have been subject to this pressure to this very day, and so I am now through his questions. Your Honours, I have stated the truth before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have allowed you to complete, in short form, what you wanted to say about the matter. Now Mr. Vasic here, you will understand, is properly asking you questions which he thinks are of relevance to his client's case. And if you could exercise your patience and deal with those questions honestly and shortly, it will help this Chamber considerably. So thank you. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's questions, did you not say that Lieutenant-Colonel Kijanovic on the 20th of November at around 1900 hours allegedly told you that he had found the bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- my answer was around 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were, therefore, unable to inform Colonel Mrksic of these killings because you were not sure whether they had indeed been committed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You asked me repeatedly about me not having taken any measures or not having uncovered dead bodies. This was the thing that I was supposed to do at dead of night, go out into the cornfield searching for corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I were to tell you that Colonel Kijanovic stated that he had never told you anything of the sort, that he never -- that he had never collected any dead bodies and that he was unable to do so because that was within the purview of the sanitisation service and that the dead bodies cannot be buried before an autopsy is conducted?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, Colonel Mrksic could have had military court during wartime. You're not listening to me. Mr. Vasic, the brigade during the war has a military court. I don't know whether Colonel Mrksic had set up a military court -- or rather, I should have said that a brigade has all the different bodies. It has a lawyer who is, I believe, even a justice on the supreme court in Serbia now. And as I had heard, they had turned over every single body.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My question to you was the following: What would you say to -- if I told you that Colonel Kijanovic had stated that he was unable to and did not, in fact, bury the dead bodies. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Kijanovic did not state this only in front of me; he stated it in front of Korica, Stosic, and other persons. If he had withdrawn his statement, then my only conclusion is that somebody must have exerted pressure on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the existence of a military court. Is a military court established only when a state of war is declared?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was at that time a state of war declared in fact?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any state of emergency, as the one that existed, for instance, in the Vukovar area or in any other area where there are war operations, there are conditions in place to create a military court. But this was not, in fact, done at the time, not only by Colonel Mrksic but by all the units that were present in the area of the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the conversation with Colonel Mrksic. If I were to tell you that my client claims that he never spoke to you that night, that he was not at the command post at all, and that the only person you could have talked to was the duty officer, who was then duty-bound to record this conversation with you in the log. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Mrksic could not have spent the night sleeping in his pyjamas when you had occasion to see what all of us were doing at the time, and I don't believe that this is what Colonel Mrksic in fact told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that Colonel Mrksic did not see you that night at his work-place?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's his right to say so, but I tell you that I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 20th of November and your visit to the hospital. We heard that you received a task from the security administration which had to do with the separation and evacuation of the prisoners of war, at the same time you also had the task which you had in fact carried out at Velepromet. Under this same assignment of the selection and evacuation of prisoners of war, is that how your visit to the hospital came about, it was part of the same assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you then have some other assignment in addition to this one that you haven't told us of?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assignments I had are the ones that I described in my statement and the ones that I told about in my evidence before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who gave you this assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I chose this assignment for myself as part of the general assignment which had to do with the uncovering of war crimes and perpetrators of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that in the hospital you came across a room where JNA soldiers were held. In connection with this, I'd like to know whether at a later stage in your conversation with Vesna Bosanac you heard that a soldier by the name of Ivan Zivkovic had been treated at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to consult the statement written by Dr. Bosanac. In this statement all the facts are mentioned which have to do with the interview on what her role and her actions within the hospital were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I wanted to remind you, in fact this particular soldier, once he recovered, joined the convoy which left the hospital for Croatia in mid-October. Do you remember this man? Does this ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But if I were to see this statement, I might remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that you toured the hospital that morning with Dr. Stanojevic. Can you tell us whether Dr. Stanojevic addressed you as "Colonel" or as "Colonel Mrksic" [as interpreted] while you were touring the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he address you as "Colonel" perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that having left the hospital you went to Velepromet once again. What time was it when you went to Velepromet again?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Velepromet in a car driven by a journalist, I believe, or some sort -- a driver that I didn't know and this was after 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what assignment took you to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went over there to meet with Branko Korica to jot down an outline of the report on the tasks we had been carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what task Branko Korica had on that day at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only found him expecting the contents of the bag that I mentioned, or the brief-case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And how did you know you were going to meet him there? Did you agree to meet there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we met -- we agreed that we would meet in Captain First Class Radivojevic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you went to Velepromet on your own basically although you were driven by a journalist. Were you not afraid in view of the threats you had experienced the night before?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard from Korica that that very morning he had left the rooms in the hospital where he was with me to go to the ground floor there to inspect the situation. When I returned to Velepromet, he told me that at one point he had been approached by a sergeant, a sniper shooter, who told him to feel lucky that he was still alive. He said that he had told him: I thought that you were Colonel Branko because that's -- then I was cautioned by others that you were not, in fact. You should feel lucky for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Korica arrest the sergeant?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Or rather, did he arrest the lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He merely told me the story and Branko Korica also told me that he had two reservists taken to custody to the military detention there. I believe this was at the time when Major Lukic was in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you take any measures to find out who the sniper shooter was in order to ensure your protection?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I rather thought that it would be best for us not to meet such a person again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What could you see in the Velepromet yard when you went there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the morning hours or when I arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there at 1200 hours, as you said.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, as far as I can remember, there were buses parked there with women on board. I don't know for how long they had been there. The driver of the Land Rover went on to the command post. He went past the Velepromet. When I entered the Velepromet compound, there was just one police -- military police officer at the gate, and then inside the compound there was a captain first class with a sub-machine-gun there by the telephone. We greeted each other; he may have even introduced himself, but I wasn't sure whether he was a member of captain -- of Colonel Mrksic's unit or whether he was from the TO staff. But nevertheless he was on duty by the phone. Through our conversation, I learned that there was a person who was interested in knowing who was in the office. The person may have been interested in me, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know what you saw in the Velepromet yard as you arrived there. Was the convoy inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The convoy was out in the street. I did not find anyone or anything in the yard that would remain in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that you enter the building and, as you put it, you were looking at your notes which were to serve to draft your report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: From the moment you entered the building, did you leave the building at some point to go out into the Velepromet yard?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All through to the moment that you explained to us when you attended the government meeting and then as you went out, saw the journalists there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were journalists or not, but I saw Tomislav Peternek with his cameras, and next to him I saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've described that bit already. I was only interested in knowing whether that was the first time you left the building after having entered it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not dare leave the premises earlier because of the threats leveled at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the brief-case and Warrant Officer Korica. Did you hand the brief-case to someone to the security administration or to the security department of the 1st Military District as well as did you convey the information you had about the brief-case?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Warrant Officer Korica to write a -- an official note about the brief-case and to state who had given him the brief-case, that it was the military police officer under Borisavljevic and to say that the brief-case had been handed over by the Chetniks. He drafted the official note, and together with the brief-case he sent it to the forward command post of Ljubisa Petkovic, Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point the colonel from Arkan's escort entered the room you were in.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starovic or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. When was that? What time was it; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what time could it have been? I believe it could have been about 1.00, perhaps a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very well. You said that after that Arkan himself entered the room. How long after the departure of the colonel did he come in?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I described how that colonel and I were trying to outwit each other, and I can describe this again if necessary. But the colonel was trying to exert psychological pressure on me. I understood him to have been asked to do so by Arkan, that I should appear in all humiliation before Arkan and report to him and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You've described that, but how long after your exchange with the colonel that he entered?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the colonel entered the room three times. He'd address me, we'd have an exchange, and then he'd go back to Arkan. And then finally after I had told him that I was the most senior person in the room and that he ought to have honoured the military rules, I said that Arkan should enter. And that was when Arkan entered and addressed me with the -- in those -- in those disparaging remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but how long was that after the colonel's entry to the room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was three or five minutes, but five minutes at most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was this the first time you saw Arkan in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again after that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How long was this conversation between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as it took us to exchange the words that I recounted in my statement. He was being abusive. He called me a madman, and he kept telling me that I would have to send those prisoners of war back to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea of how long this took altogether?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These exchanges you had with Arkan and the members of his guards unit were not exactly pleasant, were they?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the members of his guards unit.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't pleasant by any stretch of the imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that in that conversation Arkan referred to a lady called Magda who had slit the throats of 40 children?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There's something else I want to know. Before your arrival in Vukovar, officially or unofficially had you ever heard anything about a necklace being made of children's fingers, allegedly made by a man named Daruvar, or about Serb children being slaughtered in a creche in Vukovar? An Italian journalist had supposedly found out about that.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I heard from Arkan was the first I ever heard about it, about this woman named Magda slitting the throats of children. I met her at the penitentiary where she was a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would just remind you, Mr. Vasic, of the time. Be conscious that you will need to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm doing my utmost to complete within -- by the end of the first session, and I think I might just succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will succeed, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point you were invited to a government meeting. What time was this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been about 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you invite anybody else to come along?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I invited Branko Korica. I told him to watch my back. I said: Pack that bag of yours, leave it in one of the drawers, and come with me to watch my back. I had a presentment of danger, and I kept thinking to myself: What sort of a government is this and what sort of a meeting is this at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you felt there was danger, why did you go?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt I needed to go in order to keep Arkan and his guards unit from coming back, perhaps even trying to arrest me or at least mistreat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you left the room to go to the government meeting, you didn't exactly leave the building. You just took the corridor and you walked down the corridor all the way to that room where the meeting was taking place?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But on my way there I watching through that glass pane and I realised what was happening outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please try to stick to the gist of my question. I have severe time limitations imposed on me, and I'm trying to do my best with what I had. When you entered the meeting room, the meeting had not got off the ground yet and the ministers were still arriving, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to those ministers, commanders of TO staffs and chiefs of SUP were also arriving?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some at least. I recognised some of them as people in those official capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is: From the moment you entered the meeting -- or rather, how long did it take for the meeting to begin after you had entered the room?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean how long it took for the meeting to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did it begin?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they got in and then Mr. Goran Hadzic came in, and then it took three or five minutes for the rest of them to come in, the ministers, their assistants, staff commanders, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your assessment, the meeting might have started at 1300 hours or 1315 at the latest?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. I can't be much more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that the meeting was opened by Goran Hadzic who said that this was a continuation of a previous meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember him mentioning anything about the government adopting a conclusion at the previous meeting which took place on the 19th of November, 1991, to the effect that the JNA had to submit to the government of Eastern Slavonia, Srem, and Baranja for as long as they were still in their territory?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he said that. It would have struck me as very strange because, if anything, his ambition was great.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're answering questioned posed to you by the justice minister and you said you were there on behalf of the security administration, the Supreme Command, and the top level state leadership. You said that the decision had to be observed that the prisoners of war be sent to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made it crystal clear that I was there on behalf of those bodies and that the prisoners of war were to be sent to Sremska Mitrovica. And then the justice minister, Susa, asked me on whose orders I was acting. I do believe that Arkan had told them about what I had said to him previously, when he asked me the same question in a rather offensive way and when he made threats to the effect that I would be made or forced to send them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what you answered the minister who asked you about whose call it was for those prisoners to be sent back to Vukovar from Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they had been taken to Mitrovica in an organised manner, and that their return should then likewise be organised. What I meant was planning, implementation, supervision, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During your interview with the OTP investigator, did you mention the fact that at the meeting you spoke about being there with a security group on behalf of the security administration, that you had been acting on their orders, and that you had not sent away 1.500 prisoners of war, but rather as few as 800?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is if at one point in time you were addressed by Ljuban Devetak. You've mentioned that already, saying that the JNA made a Croat Stalingrad out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said hat one day all the Croatian children would learn about this and this would be used for their indoctrination. He said --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My apologies, but can you please make a pause because we keep having overlaps and there is little that eventually gets recorded.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I repeat my question. Do you remember Ljuban Devetak at this government session telling you that Vukovar -- that the JNA had made a Croatian Stalingrad out of Vukovar, and this would remain as a historical fact that would be used to indoctrinate Croatian children?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be a study case and it would be used for indoctrination. The TO would have liberated Vukovar long ago, had it not been for the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At this government meeting -- I don't mean you personally but the JNA as a whole, were any armed threats made against you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Arkan was the only one carrying a Heckler gun, a long barrel, across his chest. And he had that well-known expression, menacing expression, and he was waiting to see what would happen in order to then decide what he would do about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. I meant if any words were uttered by any of the ministers present at the meeting that an attempt would be made to prevent the taking away of prisoners by force or by the use of weapons.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those who were taken away were mentioned -- first they said there would be a vote on what would happen to me. And the next thing they said was that I would be told to bring them back from Sremska Mitrovica, to bring the prisoners back. The next thing that was said was another threat and what you've just stated and what I've pointed out already, that I would never leave that room alive. Maybe I should have said that first, that I would never leave that room alive and that there was no way we would ever be allowed to release those Ustashas and criminals from the hospital. The barracks had already been surrounded by the TO units and the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were the only officer at the meeting at this point in time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if one of them said: Colonel, don't be scared. There is another lieutenant-colonel, he should be around somewhere, but he's off on an errand or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. But what I want to know now is: Upon your return, did you draft a report about this and did you send it to the security administration to inform them that threats had been made at Vukovar against JNA members, threats made by the local authorities who tried to stand in your way? Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies to you, my apologies to the Chamber, but there's something I have to say. I have to tell you exactly what Warrant Officer Korica told me. I asked him: Why didn't you follow me into that room to watch my back? Do you know what I had to go through? And he replied: I tried to get into the room but I was stopped by Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. He also stopped another TO member who was threatening to chuck a grenade into the meeting room. Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was trying to hush the whole thing up and trying to calm down that TO member with the assistance of some military police officers. This TO member was trying to explain that they had killed his boss. His boss was the chief of Velepromet who was an ethnic Serb. There were the Chetniks, there was Marko Crevar, and it was they, as I understood at the time, who had killed an ethnic Serb who happened to be the chief of Velepromet. I don't know what the reason was, but what I gathered was that Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was within the compound at the relevant time, that was before the meeting. And he met Goran Hadzic and everybody else. Most likely Branko Korica will testify about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vujic, but you're not answering my question, are you? We'll get to this, but what I want to know now is: Did you send that report or not? Yes or no, please, it's that simple.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course I didn't. I asked all my superiors if they knew everything that had been going on, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And they all said they knew, so you decided not to file a report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they all said they knew. I believe a copy of the minutes from that particular meeting should be available it's just that I've never seen those.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll get to Lieutenant-Colonel Panic now. You've just told me that it was at this government meeting that you heard about the fact that there were people waiting for him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you've never shared this with anybody up to this point. Your earlier account was that he came to the government meeting or that he was expected and not that he returned?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each time I said that he was expected. I am saying this now before this Chamber, and I'm saying it to you so that the Chamber may be informed about this fact which I believe to be relevant because it shows that Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was there once the government people arrived. He was within the Velepromet compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that Lieutenant Panic's account is quite different. He says he was late for the start of the meeting. The meeting had already commenced by the time he got there. He said he spoke at that meeting, and you said: He got there, he came in, the ministers assembled around him, and you were left in the room all alone.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Mr. Vasic, that Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was not there with me at that meeting. I would have loved for him to be there. It was in your present that Lieutenant-Colonel Panic tried to talk me into agreeing to harmonise or coordinate our statement, to indicate that he was there at the meeting. However, the only thing I can say is: He wasn't there. He arrived just as I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long the meeting took, the government meeting, and when, roughly speaking, did it end?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have taken about 45 minutes, the duration of a block in primary school. It finished when Lieutenant-Colonel Panic came -- or rather, when the buses came. These are some facts to be taken into account. I don't know when the buses arrived from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking you about a very rough time-line. Would you say past 2.00 or at around 2.00?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd say that's a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I just object on one small matter. My learned friend is trying to put to the witness what Colonel Panic's account or statement says, and I appreciate the difficulties -- well, I presume he is, because that's the way it seems to be sloped. I see my learned friend saying no. If in actual fact he is going to be putting Colonel Panic's account to him, I've got Colonel Panic's statement here. I, for my part, have no objection at all for this witness to have paragraph 81 read to him which relates to the Velepromet meeting and see whether this witness agrees with that particular account or not rather than, perhaps, an inadvertent misrepresentation of a facts. And I don't criticise my learned friend; I only suggest this as a way to ensure that it can be done accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the witness has shown that he's familiar with what Lieutenant-Colonel Panic said and that he abides by what he said. I'm afraid that due to lack of time, every minute is precious to us, and there's nothing further I want to go into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you guide yourself. Please be aware that you've had a very generous allowance of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I feel better now. I will continue with the questions so as to keep to my schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that you said that you went to the barracks. I would like to know until what time you stayed in the barracks, approximately.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first question is when I left that place with and in the Velepromet yard I saw only a journalist, Tomislav Peternek, a photographer, and two or three others --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've already told us who was there. So we don't want to hear that, but I want to know what time you left.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about 3.00 when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the barracks? When did you leave the barracks to go to Negoslavci, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise about the time. I had lunch there. I had a conversation with Major Lukic, which went on for some time, and then be Colonel Gvero, who was getting ready to brief the minister; Rade Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us that. But when did you arrive in Negoslavci, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then I looked at the damage to the barracks. I said that I arrived in Negoslavci at around 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform were you wearing throughout your stay in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an olive-grey uniform with an officer's belt, a windcheater, a Tito cap, and a back-pack, and a small bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have a pistol?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in Negoslavci you came across members of your group. Did you also meet soldiers from the 1st Military District? Did they go back to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were around, but they didn't go back to Sid with us. They remained in the area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what their tasks were, if you know, on the 20th and where they were?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had tasks given them by the security organ in wartime, and that they reported on their work to their superiors. Colonel Petkovic or whoever it was who gave them their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us what you heard that Colonel Tomic had said to Colonel Mrksic about the fact that the TO wanted to take over the prisoners of war from the barracks by force. If I tell you that Colonel Mrksic's standpoint was that Colonel Tomic, in the presence of an air force colonel, never said anything like that to him, nor was Colonel Mrksic ever an advocate of the alleged idea that anyone should be treated with laxity, and especially not that prisoners of war should be handed over to the local authorities, what would you say to that? Did the Colonel tell you the same thing or perhaps you…

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not mistaken about what he told me…what Colonel Tomic said. I believe that Colonel Kijanovic was with him. He never left him for a moment, just as Branko Korica never left me. I believe that he went, as was his duty as the leader of our group, to report to Colonel Mrksic about the events that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were waiting for the column that was forming to go to Belgrade, and then you say you heard shots from the direction of Ovcara. Was it after 2300 hours or later?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting lasted for some time. It wasn't just a single short burst. There was a shop there, and we milled around in front of that shop and the column was forming behind us. I didn't know why we had to wait for so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, you've already explained that. I'm just interested in the time. Could that have been at around 11.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was after 10.00 p.m., towards midnight, in that span of time. That's when the shooting was heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that on your arrival in Sid to see General Babic and Colonel Petkovic and that you heard that they knew about the events that had to do with the evacuation of prisoners from Velepromet and the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you said, he was in charge of dealing with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for some kind of coordination, but I can't tell you precisely what his task was. I know what the tasks of a chief were who was holding such a post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And a general question about this. While you were travelling back to Belgrade, did you ask Colonel Tomic whether he would report to the security administration or whether you should do it? I'm referring to a written report.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vasic. Colonel Tomic went to Belgrade almost every weekend, and he went into the security administration. There was an operations duty service there. There was a war on. Some people say there wasn't a war, but there actually was a war, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My time is running out, so I have to be very quick. I have only a few more questions. After your return to Sremska Mitrovica, did you ever write any kind of report any anything that had occurred in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you took notes about all this in your notebook if you didn't write a report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how could I describe these events in my statement? You can see how long it is. This "mokraca" [phoen] that you're interested in, you can see how many people's names I had to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether Colonel Petkovic or the chief of security of the 1st Military District ever submitted a report to the chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they did, but they were duty-bound to submit regular reports, daily operations reports, just as Colonel Mrksic had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you submit any criminal reports against persons whom you knew to have committed characters in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no proof that they had committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you submit a report in writing about the fact that you allegedly informed Colonels Mrksic and Sljivancanin about the events on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained what I had experienced. I did not accuse Major Sljivancanin for performing his tasks. I told a general, whom you know well, that Major Sljivancanin would be the best witness in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. My time has almost run out. I have two more questions, so please allow me to finish. Did you submit a report in writing about the fact that you allegedly reported to Mrksic and Sljivancanin about the events of the 19th of November, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only made a statement about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Did you ever submit a written report to anyone about the events in Velepromet that allegedly took place on the 19th of November during the evacuation that you were in charge or about the government session you attended?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't report in writing; I reported orally right away to Colonel Tomic, and I told him what I had experienced at the government session. And Colonel Kijanovic and Major Slobodan Stosic and others were present when I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm asking you whether you reported in writing.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I reported orally when the chief of the security administration, Aleksandar Dimitrijevic summoned me. At the time you're interested in when I was part of the group, he was the deputy of Colonel Radivojevic. That's why I said to Dimitrijevic: You should have been where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. I hope I haven't disappointed you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. You always manage to rise to the occasion. We will now have the first break and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good day. I am Defence counsel for Miroslav Radic, as you heard, counsel Borivoje Borovic. How many years of experience do you have as a troop officer? That means experience in working with military units.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many men a company has.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: An infantry company or a motorised company in combat, is that the lowest-level tactical unit?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question: Can you tell us the difference between subordination and joint action or coordinated action?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subordination is regulated through an order, a different kind of order than coordination is. In the case of coordination, the order is to work together in carrying out a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And who?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subordinate -- the superior officer determines the area and the axis, and for operations units, the zone of attack or defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree if I tell you that during these combat operations a company leader first has an observation post, and the next highest-ranking unit has a command post? Did you have the approval of the security administration to be sent from Sid to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Sid to Vukovar, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And when did you get this approval?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Colonel Tomic could have obtained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The answer to my previous question has not been recorded. When I asked the witness: In connection with the observation post and the command post of a brigade commander and higher-ranking units, his response has not been recorded. I'll do it again for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, that's how I put my question, that a company commander establishes an observation post of the company command and that a battalion commander or a commander of higher-level units establishes a command post?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's according to the military regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you were giving your statement to the OTP -- do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And do you have the statement that you gave before the military court?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have it, but I haven't brought it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please hand this statement; it's the statement made before the military court. In case I put something to the witness, the witness will be able to read it or compare the text to my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at the statement you made to the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to give it to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Here you are. The first page of your statement, could you look at it. My question is: Who was with you when you were making this statement? Did you have someone giving you advice or did you give the statement on your own?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the persons who were present included Gradomir [phoen] Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also colonel -- just let me see. Colonel Mojsilovic from the military part of the commission on cooperation with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
