utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, two persons were with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the name of this other officer, is it on the front page of this witness interview?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In 2002 this person, you say, was an officer cooperating with The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other person was a member of the commission, the military part of the commission headed by a general. There was some retired generals in the commission, maybe one or two active ones, and there was Colonel Mojsilovic as the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time you made the statement and when you say this friend of yours, Miletic, as it says on the front page, was he a soldier or was he the director of a company called Smederevka?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the director of that company but he used to be a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you then explain to Their Honours how the director of a company dealing in fruit juices and fruit and vegetables can be part of such a high-level commission cooperating with The Hague and be present during your interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miletic used to be a judge of the military court in Zagreb. After that, he was a major in the legal service, in the legal administration of the SSNO. After he left the army, he became the director of that company. But he is a graduate lawyer and he was an attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he an attorney at the time you were making the statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What it says here was that he was there as a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will comment on this at another time. Let us now go back to our main topic. Did Colonel Radivojevic issue a specific order to you? He was your immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that he gave me general tasks. I asked him whether this was covered legally, if you understand me, and he said: There is an order on organising camps for prisoners of war and collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And his recommendation for your work, what did it say?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that we were to investigate crimes and criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Aleksandar Vasiljevic, whom we have mentioned in these proceedings, did he issue any specific orders?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see Aleksandar Vasiljevic until the arrival in KP Dom in Sremska Mitrovica when we communicated by telephone occasionally He issued tasks to me or received reports from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see Aleksandar Vasiljevic before you came to make this statement here?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, except when I was interviewed as a witness by the investigating judge of the Novi Sad district court. I think his name is Alen Pijevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Alen Pic.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Alen Pic. And he was doing that on the premises of the military court in Proleterskih Brigada Street which has been renamed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was this meeting like with Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was also being interviewed as a witness, as far as I could tell, and so we encountered each other in the waiting-room where there were other witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As we have heard over these past few days, you helped - I'm using your own words - to evacuate prisoners and take them to Sremska Mitrovica. And for the most part, this was what your activity entailed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Haven't we heard that your task was to investigate war crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. War crimes have to be investigated pursuant to the rules. I can't remember the precise article now. You'll know that better than I do. And we start this procedure only after prisoners of war are evacuated to a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you did not take any suspect interviews from any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the ground in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you didn't take any statements in Vukovar, why were you present there as someone in charge of investigating war crimes? You say that there were enough people from the military police and other companies to evacuate the prisoners, so what were you doing out on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you have observed the duality of command in Velepromet. This is a salient characteristic of the relations between the Territorial Defence and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you draw up an official note about this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I acted as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you draw up an official note at the government session, as you said?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only tried to write down some key words, and because I did that I received threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where is your official note now?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't exist anymore. This was a notepad that I as a security organ carried around with me, and I believe it has been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you mean when you say you believe it has been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documentation I, as a security organ, handed over remained in a file or a dossier or a binder referring to the case I was working on. It contained all my notes and the statements I took from prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You had an official logbook and a case you were working on. Can you clarify this to avoid misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a single case. My work in the Sremska Mitrovica KP Dom took place from the 21st of November to the 27th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, to clarify this further, I see you're giving very precise answers, so let's continue like this. My -- you said that your official note and log-book were probably in that case file. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case file, in that dossier, my notes remained there. That was a dossier concerning my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And this file of yours relating to Sremska Mitrovica, was it sent to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was received by the next camp commander and his subordinates. I remember that when I was sitting there, at one point in time I felt someone leaning against my chair behind my back. When I turned around, I was surprised to see someone I knew. I couldn't recall who he was, but he looked familiar. It was Major Srecko Borisavljevic, and there was another major, Major Luka Miljus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember what my question was?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're looking for my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that it's in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As someone who gave himself a task, as we have just heard, can you tell us how many members of the ZNG were hiding in the hospital, the paramilitary formation, approximately.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unable to check that, and it was not my task to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you establish that members of the ZNG and the Croatian paramilitary formations were hiding in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one example. When a member of the Territorial Defence brought before me a man whom he said was a criminal, and he told me that his nickname was Jajo or Joja. And he said that he had slaughtered Serbs; he gave me some examples of his crimes. And I first said --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So there was one example.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only that one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Before your arrival in the hospital, did you have any knowledge that during the last days of the Vukovar operations the Crisis Staff had moved to the hospital and operated from there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that first from Major Sljivancanin when he briefed us. After that, I had an interview with Dr. Vesna Bosanac and I asked her about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You, as we heard, introduced yourself as Colonel Branko in various places. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In some statements or parts of your statement you even asked people to introduce themselves to you - is that correct - officers or non-commissioned officers with whom you communicated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the commander of the armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My next logical question is as follows. On page 11, line 1 of your statement to the OTP, did you say that the buses escorted by armoured combat vehicles left the Velepromet compound?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You have the statement before you. Did you say that there was a colonel at the head of the column?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be logical for you to ask that colonel to introduce himself to you because then that would constitute the end of your task? You would then have known to whom you handed over those people, and you would be able to include that in your report, whether oral or written?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us then.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have liked it to have been like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, whose omission was it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the omission of more than one colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the hospital, you said that you found a military police company there.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found a unit of the military police there providing security for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know what the name of the commander of the military police company was?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I can only tell you what Major Sljivancanin had said, that they had been rotating.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the part of your statement wherein you said -- my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in line 7 -- oh, now it's fine. The transcript has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You stated: I gave myself the assignment at the hospital. That was in line 12 -- or, rather, page 12, line 4 of your statement to the OTP, and I believe you repeated that part of the statement here?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If there are any such regulations, then you will have to tell me which regulations these were, allowing you to give yourself assignments on your own. You said that in the area covering [as interpreted] by Colonel Mrksic, that there was no one else who could issue orders than him, or were you the person number one at that point and you did not need the authorisation of any officer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not consider myself to be in charge there. I said before -- in front of Major Sljivancanin and others present there that I wanted to inspect the way in which the hospital was used from the perspective of the international laws of war, its use and abuse, and that I was to interview the POWs and any other suspects in view of the possible commission of crimes, that I wanted to take stock of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you did not say "I wished to," you said "I assigned myself the task."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked who had given that assignment to me, and I could have said that this was pursuant to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If this was pursuant to the law, then it's all fine. In the statement you gave to the OTP you have before you on page 13, line 2 -- please find the page, page 13.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 13, line 2, "on the roof," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question is as follows: You stated there that on the roof of the hospital there were traces of the presence of this armed formation there. Before that, you referred to the ZNG formations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to describe in more detail for the Trial Chamber, since you were acting in accordance with the law, what sort of presence you established there in terms of the strength, equipment, ammunition, and action of the unit.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No ammunition or equipment was found there. First of all, Dr. Stanojevic stated that a unit was stationed there which was subordinated to the big boss, as he put it, Bojler, Veliki Bojler, who was the commanding officer of the ZNG unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, line 19, question and answer have been shown as a question only. So they should be split. That's line 16 -- from line 19 the answer starts, but it seems to be continuous text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that's enough or should we put the same question to the witness again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stanojevic tell you that members of the ZNG had used this vantage point under the roof in the attic to observe?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they removed tiles. The attic was covered only by beams and tiles. If you removed some tiles, you would -- you were able to see the surroundings of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the tiles had been removed only on this one spot?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had their own room where they were located, and obviously this other spot was their observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on two places only you found traces of their observation posts where the ZNG formations were located?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You also stated in paragraph 5 on page 13, the last two lines --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: -- That nobody in the hospital was wounded or killed by shelling. All the wounded had been brought in from combat positions.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In carrying out your task, that's the inspection you conducted, did you find any traces of leftover weapons or did you hear of any discarded weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before me there were members of the military police who entered the hospital, and it must have been in their interest to collect any such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you allow then for the possibility that had there been any -- if there were any weapons they were taken away by them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On page 15 of your statement for the OTP in paragraph 1. Have you found this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You state that you started making notes for your report. My question to you is: For the report intended for whom?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who precisely?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: His name, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vasiljevic. Although I never sent my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that after these answers you have to explain for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I was not asked to submit any such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you unhappy about the fact that you were not asked to submit such a report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you frustrated to a certain extent on that account?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite some time has passed since, and I was interviewed on these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you were -- were you angry about this at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In view of your extensive involvement and the many years of your work that you investigated, did you expect to be retired from the rank of a general?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not expect that and I regarded my work with modesty. I believed that my work was important to inform the military leadership on significant matters for the decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But in view of the procedure and in view of the tasks you accomplished, would it not have been appropriate for you to have retired from the rank of a general?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not regard myself in that light.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Branko, is that the name you used only for the purposes of the Vukovar assignment or --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only for the time I worked with the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But can you then explain the following: In December 2002, when you gave the statement to OTP, why does the statement contain your name [as interpreted] as Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the investigators had asked me whether I had had a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's not the way the statement is put at all. He gives his name perfectly clearly, and then the statement says in nickname/alias: Colonel Branko. The name is quite clear. His name is quite specific there. No attempt to mislead whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an error in the transcript. My question was "nickname," whereas the transcript says "name." My learned friend is partly right to say that, but my question included the term "nickname," not the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my full name and surname are contained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we should not have any confusion here unnecessarily. I asked why his nickname, that's to say, that of Colonel Branko, featured here again 11 years later. Does it mean that you had other code-names?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the statements I took from Dr. Bosanac, from Dr. Sadika Bilus, from Mirko - I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We are wasting time. In 2002 you, yourself, stated that your nickname was Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this was the nickname that you used widely and was generally known?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't generally known. It served only this purpose, and the statement I gave was used in the Milosevic case, when Milosevic himself showed my statement to Dr. Bosanac, when she testified in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the transcript, page 4559, and not the page you're looking at, not the page 2 to 5 [as interpreted], but rather the transcript of your evidence here. On that page, lines 2 to 5, you state -- you stated that they became prisoners the moment they raised their hands and laid down their weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since you agree with this, my question is as follows: During the time of your stay in Vukovar, did you at any point see anyone raise their hands or lay their weapons down?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the government meeting, how come you knew that the person chairing the meeting was called Ilija Kucarevic [phoen]? When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met him many years before that in Novi Sad. I knew another cabinet member there; that was Vojislav Vukcevic, a doctor of law. I believe you know him as well. He was present at the government meeting too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I find this information precious for private purposes, but let's move on. As is stated on page 17, line 10 in this statement to the OTP, is it true that when you were asked at the government meeting -- please find the page before I move on. Therefore, page 17, line 10.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 17, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You -- "I answered that my name was Colonel Branko and that I was there with a group of security organs, for which we were tasked by the chief of the security administration and I stated that we had acted upon his orders and plan." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did the chief of the security administration inform you of the plan related to Vukovar or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On page 20 --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If I may add, I did not finish saying that I had met Mr. Vukcevic as early as in 1974 on the solemn occasion when a bridge was inaugurated, was made operational. It was a bridge symbolising brotherhood and unity of the 51st Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but we have to save time. Can you find page 20 of your statement to the OTP. Would you please be so kind as to read out the first line.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Those who provided security to Velepromet" -- oh, "all of us were waiting -- we kept waiting for something."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you seemed to have been waiting for something, and then you heard shots from the direction of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that Negoslavci are at least five kilometres away from Ovcara as the crow flies, or if I were to tell you that Negoslavci are more than five and a half kilometres away from Grabovci, would this not mean that you were not able to hear shots from those directions?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were, Mr. Borovic. And expert witnesses would be better placed to explain this both to you and to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I consulted experts, and --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they must have deceived you. I am a tank operator by --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You stated: "I don't know, but we seemed to be waiting for something." And my question to you is: Were you waiting for your mission to be accomplished?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was only later that I realised that Vesna Bosanac was in the column as well as was the group that arrived later on at Metkovci [phoen], and I believed that we were waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn later on what it was that you were waiting for?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who told you to wait?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody did, except for the person who was to issue orders for the column to move ahead. And I don't know to this day who it was who should have issued an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any official note from Velepromet or from the barracks or from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any such official notes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had the notebooks that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned a notebook, and now you're mentioning "notebooks."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have these notepads, you see, such as this one. I, for instance, was writing down the questions put to me by Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you establish how many JNA officers were killed in Vukovar after all these events?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that, except that I was able to read in the press that there were more than one victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Victims of -- which victims?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Victims who were soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very well -- very much. Do you know who Captain Nikolic from Sremska Mitrovica is? Captain Mitrovic [as interpreted], and I'm referring to the period you stayed at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know who Major Mitrovic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us who he is.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a major wearing an air force uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, there is a mistake in the transcript. It says "Major Mitrovic," whereas it should say "Major Nikolic." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a member of the security body from the security administration under Aleksandar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think that's right. I think your answer is correct. My question is: Did Major Nikolic process all of your reports, and I don't mean just the people from Sremska Mitrovica, and take them straight to Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were I to tell you that some of the witnesses in relation to these facts said that this was indeed the case, would you allow for the possibility that someone took these reports to him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Because he was also attached to the other team, the team that remained in the area after we had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said you went to the hospital with Major Sljivancanin in a vehicle you described as P-U-H, PUH [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's an all-terrain vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said there was another officer with you. My question is: Was he a security officer? Was he a military police officer? Was he one of the escort?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Warrant Officer Branko Korica, a security officer from Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic's group or from General Mile Babic's group. He was subordinated to either of those two officers. He used to be one of my subordinated officers back when I was still an officer with the counter-intelligence group attached to the army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It would have been impossible for another officer from a totally different unit to be there in that vehicle with you on your way to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It could only have been one of the officers under Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and track down page 14 of your statement to the OTP. There were no questions about this by the OTP. I am looking at paragraph 2. Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When asked by the Prosecutor whether I knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But please, read it out slowly because you haven't testified about this yet.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When asked by the investigator, Vladimir Dzuro, whether I knew Captain Radic, I am positive that nobody by that last name ever introduced himself to me, nor was I ever in touch with such a person, except for what I've already stated. There was another officer with Major Sljivancanin in the PUH vehicle with no rank, or at least none that I noticed. I saw him with the soldiers near the hospital at the time when I handed over that flak jacket. I was not aware of the fact that this was Captain Radic."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you seem quite determined as far as Captain Radic's role is concerned, I have to ask you again, please try to be crystal clear about it. You did not see Captain Radic anywhere in or near the hospital compound, and he certainly wasn't in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, even though I never adduced any evidence of it for obvious reasons. If my learned friend has elicited the fact and indeed the witness has said that he doesn't know who Captain Radic is, how on earth can he possibly say he was or was not there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Borovic, the witness can go no further than to say that he wasn't aware of a Captain Radic being present, but it is his very specific evidence that he didn't know Captain Radic. So he cannot tell you that somebody standing around wasn't Captain Radic. If there are other people there, he doesn't know who they were. He doesn't Captain Radic, so I think you won't be able to go further than that. He was not aware of Captain Radic being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I deliberately spoke about this captain along these lines. If it's not the one who was in the PUH vehicle, if that wasn't Captain Radic, then perhaps not. But the witness has made himself crystal clear about this issue, and there's no need to pursue it. I think you're entirely you're right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm just conferring with my learned friend. She's noticed something in the transcript. What the statement says and what the witness has just read out on the transcript is not identical. The statement says that the person had no rank. This was misread by the witness, perhaps, or it's been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So which is true?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I didn't note any ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was the crime in relation to which you interrogated Vesna Bosanac at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interrogating her about possible crimes at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you interrogating her about a crime that is normally described as a war crime?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in no position to do anything like that. I was asking her the questions that as a security officer I was entitled to ask. This is at the investigation stage of the proceedings before charges are even brought against a person. You try to establish facts about crimes that may or may not have been committed. I was asking her questions about dead bodies, who they were, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the Chamber and in order to shed light on your work at Mitrovica, I must ask you this: Are you aware of the existing legal regulations on the distinction between grounds for suspicion and founded suspicion?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that distinction, and this distinction is very important for any investigative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in order to file a criminal complaint, it is sufficient for there to be grounds for suspicion?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in order to start an investigation it is necessary to establish that there are grounds for suspicion against someone?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that not mean that no criminal complaint in relation to Vukovar was filed because there were no grounds to suspect any persons of having committed crimes to begin with?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The grounds for suspicion were assessed by the relevant prosecutor of the military court -- or the military prosecutor. At the time I believe this was Lieutenant-Colonel Mladenovic who held an MA degree in law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is an area that we're both familiar with. My learned friend Vasic asked you whether you pressed charges against anyone because of what had occurred in Vukovar, and your answer was: No, I didn't because there wasn't sufficient evidence. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what I'm asking you now is the existence of evidence, on the one hand, and grounds for suspicion on the other. There's quite a difference there between the two, isn't there? Does that mean that you did not file any criminal complaints because there were no grounds for suspicion, or was this something that your legal officer should have done?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer a question like this. You need to know something about the way our work was organised. You had to take into account the role of the investigating magistrate. At this time, it's Miodrag Salic, attorney-at-law. Back then he was working together with Major Stankovic, a pathologist, and head of a ward at the military hospital in Belgrade. He carried out autopsies on all dead bodies that were found in the area. These needed to be traced back to any remaining members of the family who were still alive. You know that that was no easy task at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would eye-witness statements not be taken into account when these reports were being drafted? Did you have anything in writing in terms of witness statements regarding the circumstances of these crimes before you spoke to the investigating magistrate?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such thing. I carried the investigation out myself. Just to give you an example --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prisoner of war, whenever there was a commander, as ZNG called them, I would ask them: What about your defence area, was anybody killed in your defence area? Were there any dead people? Were there any dead bodies? And they would say: Yes. During the night somebody brought two bodies into our area from a different defence area. What did you then do, I would ask them. And then the person would say: We would burn them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Your answer is very clear. We know about JNA bodies being burned -- bodies of JNA soldiers being burned at Borovo Komerc, we've heard about that. But my question now is: Did you look into the matter, into the circumstances, because your remit was quite comprehensive, wasn't it? Did you look into any crimes possibly committed by members of the JNA? What you're telling us now. Did you take statements from anybody in the JNA or any other military unit in the area, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no chance to speak to anybody from the JNA. I wanted to speak to soldiers who had been captured in order to find out more about the circumstances because there are a number of wounded there, too. I wanted to know more about the circumstances, and those soldiers were heard and statements were taken from them by Colonel Kijanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the time when you finished your report, which Major Nikolic may or may not have taken to the security administration, did these reports ever go missing from the administration files or were these reports forwarded to any judiciary bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe these reports were eventually passed on to the judiciary bodies. First an assessment would be made about the possible relevance of a statement, in as far as statements indicated the existence of crimes and perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As for Sremska Mitrovica, you said today, and I believe you said the same thing yesterday but I can always go back to your statement for us to verify this, you said that Vojin Susa, the justice minister in that government, brought along five or six lawyers who were "the authors of our work in Sremska Mitrovica"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what do you have to say? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should have gone back to my first statement when I said Vojislav Susa, when he asked me: Can we have other bodies attending the process, attending these interviews when security officers are interviewing prisoners of war? I said: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But first of all you need to get approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I need to stop you right there. There's a question that may be of relevance of the Defence, and then you tend to speed up and provide very comprehensive answers in order to lose track of the original question. It may be an accidental thing. I don't believe -- I don't wish to believe that you're doing this deliberately. I'm asking you: Is it true that Vojin Susa, the justice minister of the Krajina SAO, Baranja, and Zaparanje [phoen], Srem, sent monitors to Sremska Mitrovica to keep tabs on your work?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they helped uncover criminals of war. And Vojin Susa personally was there and he helped us track down war criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who authorised him to monitor you, a security officer, on an important and very secret mission on behalf of the security administration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps it may be the interpretation. I suspect it is that. It's "to keep tabs on your work." Is that in the plural or is that in the singular? It does seem later on that it does go into the singular, but can we just have that clarified because it may be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying singular or plural of tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I'm saying singular or plural of -- 66.13, "to keep tabs on your work," because the work related to a group of people at Sremska Mitrovica. Is it "your" in the plural or "your" in the singular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I see what you mean. On the work of this witness personally --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- Or the work of the group --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- The group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- of which this witness was a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's worthy of some clarification, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That group comprises five or six lawyers, the group established by Vojin Susa, the justice minister in the SAO Krajina government, did they keep tabs on your work, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could take it to mean that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did he personally monitor your work?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could have taken it to mean that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did they personally take part in the sorting out --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... same point. "Your" means plural or singular in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue is whether it is somebody just watching this person here, who is the witness, Mr. Vujic, or whether it is somebody watching the work of the group there. "Your" is a word in English that can mean both in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Thank you. It was with respect that I used the plural. I don't think Mr. Moore understands the distinction in our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question: Was the work of all the investigators at Sremska Mitrovica being monitored by this group established by the justice minister, Vojin Susa, or was the work of Colonel Branko or Bogdan Vujic alone being monitored?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my work being monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the other investigators?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Don't yell.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you have to respect me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My only question about this is: Who authorised Vojin Susa to monitor you in carrying out security work?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the camp commander, he informed me that Goran Hadzic had first come to the camp together with minister Vojin Susa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that he asked for Aleksandar Vasiljevic. He said to him that Vasiljevic wasn't there, that he was probably in Belgrade. Then they uttered a threat to the effect that they would lose their general. I asked Colonel Maksimovic: What is this about? He said: They arrived here and they were very upset. They came to the KP Dom Sremska Mitrovica, probably to see the director or the warden. They had received approval to enter the premises where the commander was and where the offices were. And they made a threat, referring to General Vasiljevic. He asked: What is this about? But they wouldn't say at the time. He sent them to Belgrade to look for Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Whether they found him or whether they obtained approval for Vojin Susa and his group to attend, I don't know, but he monitored my personal work, and I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Was this the first time in your career that someone was monitoring you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, monitoring is quite legal and normal. It's an institution of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The government of the SAO Krajina, was it part of the chain of command in respect to the security organs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear when I said that duality with respect to Article 112 was evident first in Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that there were two commands -- two chains of command. Who was behind them, I don't know. Don't ask me. You can try to clarify that with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujic. It's evident that there were parallel chains of command, one in Vukovar and one in Belgrade headed by Aleksandar Vasiljevic. And when proceedings had to be instituted under every law, he gave permission for your investigations to be monitored and controlled.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's misrepresentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Moore. The witness said something quite different. You are adding in your understanding, Mr. Borovic, which is not that of the witness. You will have to get the witness's understanding, if you want it, and that's as far as this witness can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Very well. The conclusion is premature, but my question is as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that in Sremska Mitrovica, that is in Serbia, there was work being carried out in parallel on this investigation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not how I would put it. I told you that my work was monitored by Minister Vojislav Susa and his lawyers, some of whom were judges in the Vukovar court or in some other court on that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that they could get authorisation to do that from the chief of the security administration. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe they could have obtained permission from some other ministry, because I told you that at least two ministries gave their approval for the establishment of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Defence which was actually called the Federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice headed by this Susa, what was it responsible for at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it was their prisoners of war, not just the prisoners of war of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: According to the code on criminal procedure, do you know he could not have had that authorisation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you understood me correctly, he pressured me to say what laws we would be working under, and I told him we would be applying the laws of the federal state and implementing the federal law on criminal procedure. He asked: Why not the law on criminal procedure of Serbia? And I just looked at him in surprise. I said: There is a state called the SFRY, and there is the JNA. And the JNA worked under federal laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you've answered what was to be my next question. You were working under federal laws at the time. Did you take any steps against Vojin, or Vojo, as you called him, Susa because of his attack on your authority and your work as an investigator before he received authorisation, or were you not applying the law and not taking any steps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't draw these conclusions, please. You are exaggerating. You're going too far. Vojin Susa is a colleague of yours. I believe that you have met him. Counsel Vasic has met him. There he is. He's laughing, see? I can prove that he met him. Why don't you ask Counsel Vasic about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but your manner is really that of a security man. You're evading my questions. I'm not trying to exert any pressure on you, but I asked you whether you acted in compliance with the law. If someone is obstructing an investigation you are in charge of, why don't you arrest him or remove him, or is it like the Velepromet incident? You simply get out of the way, leaving the victims to their fate?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long time has elapsed since the war was waged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the National Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal provided you with documents before you testified?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What were these documents and when did you receive them? Could you just list them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't, actually. I received a summons to go and be handed these -- or rather, the summons for an interview. And along with that, I received a document headed "the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federal Ministry of Justice." There's a number and a date, the 4th of November, 2002 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, if necessary, I can give this document to the gentleman for him to read. But the purpose of the document is that the Federal Ministry of Justice is warning Srecko Borisavljevic, Bogdan Vujic, and Ljubisa Vukasinovic that they have been handed summons and signed receipts are mentioned as well as the statement that these persons are not exempt from the duty of keeping state and military secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What other documents did you receive, apart from this summons? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An invitation to an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview took place on the premises of The Hague offices in Jevrem Grujica Street in Dedinje. I was interviewed by the Prosecutor who is here now about my statement and my testimony before the special court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did the interview last?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted about two hours, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And were any records drawn up? Was a statement written out?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. The Prosecutor can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that lawyers Nikola Barovic, lawyer Petovar can speak about your work?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only concerning the case where they were Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what case was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the case tried, and it related to terrorism and conspiracy to carry out the crime of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And who are accused?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers of Albanian and Slovenian and Croatian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No ethnic Serb?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Before testifying here, did you cooperate with Natasa Kandic? You know who she is?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have met Mrs. Natasa Kandic. I met her in the corridor of the special court during the break, and the victims and aggrieved parties from the Vukovar area --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you cooperate with her?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to avoid a conversation with Mrs. Kandic and the citizens who were there from the Vukovar area. They were trying to put various questions to me. At one point I entered the hall during the break, and the security men were surprised to see me doing that. I realised I was being put under pressure, that they wanted to ask me about the missing and the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And Natasa Kandic was there in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood her to be a Defence attorney, somebody's counsel appearing for the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're a professional. Victims don't have defence counsel. She can only be a person who has been authorised by the victims.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Probably a good time for a break, is it, Mr. Lukic? Yes. We will resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- And to you, Mr. Vujic. I am Lukic, and I am counsel for Sljivancanin. I will be putting questions to you and you know the request of Their Honours when it comes to cross-examination. I will try to put very clear questions to you, and I would like you to give me very concise answers. If I will wish you to say something in more detail, then I will ask you to do so, and at any rate you will have the opportunity when

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This pause was meant to show you how long the interpretation takes. I will give you a factual conclusion in the form of a question, that's the following. During your testimony here and on the basis of your statement, I understood you to mean -- to say that you saw my client the last time on the 20th of November at about 1200 hours when you left the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: You did not see him on that day, either at Velepromet or at the barracks or at the government meeting or at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Except that one of the witnesses before the special court in Belgrade stated that Mr. Sljivancanin was at this meeting instead of me.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this, Witness. And both the Prosecution and I are aware of this. You were at this meeting from its beginning to its end, and you did not see Sljivancanin there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me: When was it that you received this request from the Prosecution to appear as a witness here? And I'm not talking about the statement now. I'm just talking about the time when they got in touch to call you to come here.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact answer, but I will provide you with the following explanation. I was first invited to the SUP on the 29th of November, and it was there that an inspector or a representative of the service handed me the summons for an interview. I signed a paper there confirming that I received the summons and the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Let's make it short. Did you receive a request to come to testify here from the Prosecution before the start of trial?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Based on your role and the position you had in the people's Yugoslav army, I take it that you understood Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Gvero, and Mr. Jerko Crmaric from before, even Major Lukic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand -- as far as I take it you mentioned Mr. Pavkovic first. I met him at the school for national defence; that was the war school. I probably attended his graduation ceremony and he was probably the best in his class. Which year that was, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: What about the others?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Jerko Crmaric from the security department of the first army. That's what it was -- that's how it was organised at the time. It was the command of the first army. We worked there together. He was my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: I'm just interested in knowing whether you knew him,

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew Major Lukic from before as well, from the Pancevo barracks where we spent three years working in the same barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: And you knew Milan Gvero as well?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him from the graduate military school centre, where we were members of the collegium of the chief of the centre. Colonel-General Slavomir Djokic, who passed away.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Please answer with a yes or no. And Jerko Crmaric died as well?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's still alive.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I only spoke of General Djokic.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Very well. When my learned friend from the OTP was putting questions to you on the first day, that's page 4480, on the 16th of February, he called your group as a group of senior officers. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't understand what you asked.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: When Prosecutor Moore put questions to you during his chief, he qualified you as a group of senior officers.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were officers of high ranks. Colonel is a high rank.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that you were invited into this group as a person with great professional experience for the matters that the group was expected to work on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: On several occasions you explained to my colleagues what, in your opinion, the task of the group was. I was reading the transcript and I will try to put it in a nutshell. You stated that the task of your group was to, in accordance with the international laws of war and federal regulations, work with the POWs and to make -- conduct investigations on possible war crimes.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I wish to add the following. It was only at the Sremska Mitrovica camp that it was possible to conduct identification, which doesn't mean that there weren't any persons there who used other names. Many of them did not have any identity papers. One had to establish their identity. It was in that context where perhaps Justice Minister Susa gave his contribution. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Once you explained this to my learned friend from the OTP and to colleague Vasic, I don't want to go into that, you said that this referred primarily to the members of the Croatian paramilitary formations but that you had the task to investigate war crimes and possibly war criminals, and that was your jurisdiction, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: When I saw that your work also included women, that went also for Dr. Bosanac, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: You will agree with me that under the then-regulations in Yugoslavia, all persons above the age of 16 were subject to the laws. That means those persons who are above 16.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: And this age limit is identical for the persons who are considered to be of military age. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: As a security organ, you were entitled to verify the identity of the person, to interrogate the person before any criminal proceedings are instituted?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the procedure is somewhat more specific when it comes to war criminals.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: My apologies. I established that in December 1991 you were 58. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Before that, you were retired, as you told us, but in accordance with the law on the military obligation you were also a military-aged person?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under Article 119 where -- this applies to Colonel Tomic Slavko, for instance, and Mr. Tomic because this particular article provides for the meaning of the term "volunteer" and the relation in which this term stands when it comes to an active military serviceman and a reserve military serviceman.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Let us not place too much of a difficulty for the interpreters this late in the night. Slavko Tomic was more or less the same age. You said that -- my question to you is: Had you refused Radivojevic's invitation to join the group, would there have been any consequences for you since you were an officer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this would not have been regarded in a positive light, just as the fact that I am a Prosecution witness is not regarded in a positive light. I was also offered to be a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: That wasn't my question; my question was something completely different. I apologise. At any rate, a conscript, including a reserve officer who is called to report to his unit or to report according to an assignment, if he refuses to respond to that call will incur certain sequences under the law?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 119 deals with the military personnel that has not been given any wartime assignment. I believe that I had a wartime assignment which was that in the security bodies, that was something I could assume, and I was listed of course in the military records of the relevant organ in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: You gave quite a few answers to questions requiring military expertise, and I will have to put such questions as well, and I suppose you can understand that in view of my client's function. I suppose you know very well what the relationship between the military police and the security organs is?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Do you know - and if you do, please give us a very brief answer - what sort of military police formations existed in the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I will have to give you a brief introduction. I knew Major Sljivancanin when he was company commander in the command of the defence of the city of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: You mean of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had never met. We -- our paths crossed each other professionally, and his superior, Colonel Djordjevic, had a very good opinion of Major Sljivancanin, who was captain at the time. I know Major Sljivancanin as commander of a military police battalion carried out very technical matters from the purview of the military police in providing security to important institutions.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: I will have to chide with you now. You haven't answered my question. Can you tell me which is the highest military police unit?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Who commands a military police unit in both wartime and peacetime?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer is assigned based on his individual deployment and assignment and within the overall command structure. As far as the military aspect is concerned, he is subordinated to the commander of a joint unit which he is part of. In terms of technical responsibility, he is responsible to the relevant security body.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Under the law, it's the security body that is in charge of all the technical aspects of the work of the military police. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: When a security body calls a military police officer with a request, this officer, does he need to receive approval from his superior commander about that task or assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as far as I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: But we're not there yet. I'm asking you a very general question.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please run that past me again, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: If a security body has a request to make or certain activities to be undertaken by the military police, what about the military police officer? Would he not have to receive approval from his own superior in the command structure?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the security body would request such approval from the unit commander, the most senior commander, if you like.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: You've provided two answers and I only asked one question. I think we're getting better and better all the time. Do you know if approximate during combat operations local commanders are signed or appointed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Local commanders, during combat operations unit commanders are appointed, and they're each assigned their own areas of responsibility, if we're dealing with brigade-unit levels and up. Battalions are assigned a zone.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vukovar, you -- did you report to Mrksic or did you know about the fact that Vukovar broke down into three zones and that each zone had a local commander depending on the area in question, geographically speaking? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Do you know what duties a local commander would have had?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to get a reference point for these combat areas, which makes it very difficult for me to answer your question. All we're talking about in a war is the zones of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the peculiar structure of the JNA guards brigade with its peculiar mission or, to put a leading question, what the primary mission of the guards brigade in both peace and war be to protect state officials, military officials, and commands?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give you an answer, but it may not be a competent answer. All I can say about this is that in peacetime a brigade's task is well known, or of this particular brigade. It provides security for persons and institutions which are guarded or protected in an organised manner under the law.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: I think you confirmed this yesterday, although I see you weren't precisely aware of it, but you didn't challenge this. There were two military police battalions that were part of the guards brigade, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with their structure or the way they were organised; therefore, I can hardly be expected to provide a very accurate answer. But if you're interested in this sort of information, you can go back to their annual in 2000, which reflects all of the information that you're after. There should be an accurate breakdown there about all these things you're asking me about. I don't know if there is, but I suppose there would be.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: A couple of questions about something you happen to be more familiar with. The security administration. I will read out to you Article 18 of the rules governing the work of the security bodies in the JNA. I assume that you probably know this by heart, most of these provisions at least. Can you please tell me: Did you act in keeping with these rules? "Security organs of the superior command unit or staff of the armed forces are in charge of the technical aspect of the work of the security organs of the subordinated units, institutions, and staffs of the armed forces. They assist these bodies, they organise these bodies, they direct the work of these bodies, they coordinate the work of these bodies, and they monitor the work of these bodies." If you look at this Article, if you look at what you've been talking about, generally speaking, you arrived in Vukovar. What implication did that have for the security body of the guards brigade? What was the professional relationship between your own group -- your own group is all that I'm interested in. It may be the same as the 3rd -- as the 1st Army Group. Was everything done according to regulations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In wartime, as opposed to peacetime, establishment-wise, even battalions and divisions have security bodies in the person of their commander. This goes without saying. What also goes without saying is that Major Sljivancanin had a security body in each of his battalions at the time, but they were in charge of intelligence, too. They were in charge of both intelligence and security as a body. If this was the case, this was perfectly in keeping with the wartime regulations. I am talking as if this was a fact, although I don't actually know. I did realise Borisavljevic was, on the one hand, a unit commander, a commanding officer, and on the other a security officer. I also viewed Major Sljivancanin as both a military police commander and a security officer subordinated to Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: But I didn't get my answer, did I? Please try to focus on what I'm asking you. I've read this Article back to you. It's Article 18 of the rules governing the work of security bodies. You are a member of the security body from a superior command, the security administration. It's a superior body. Technically speaking, do you assist, coordinate, and direct the work of the security bodies belonging to a lower level of command?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to you is: This was not my assignment -- or rather, I had no such assignment nor was I ever authorised to carry out an assignment like that. I was there to help evacuate the POWs.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: That was the specific mission that you had. I am asking you about these general regulations.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no assignment pursuant to the regulation you quoted, Article 18 of the rules governing the work of security bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: Isn't that supposed to be a permanent task for every commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the task of the superior officer, Major Sljivancanin, and he should know who did this job in the federal secretary's cabinet or in the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: In terms of all the technical aspects, would the security administration be superior to any other security body?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please go and ask the same question of General Vasiljevic when he appears here before this Court as a witness, if he does.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION TO ADD
utterances.text: So you know for a fact that he is about to appear and testify here, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
